nodes.label: PERMA Model
nodes.author: Seligman
nodes.summary: Happiness is not just pleasure, but balance of five dimensions: Positive Emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Achievement.
nodes.desc: The PERMA model is the core theoretical framework of positive psychology, dividing well-being into five core elements. P (Positive Emotion) — experiencing joy and happiness; E (Engagement) — flow state of complete absorption; R (Relationships) — positive social connections; M (Meaning) — belonging to something greater; A (Achievement) — pursuing goals and having a sense of accomplishment.
examples: Xiao Ming smiles every day but feels empty — only positive emotion, lacking meaning and achievement
Fully engaged at work, has good friends, feels life has meaning, feels accomplished after completion — PERMA in balance
nodes.selfTest: Rate each dimension (1-10): Positive Emotion / Engagement / Relationships / Meaning / Achievement. Total >40 indicates balanced well-being. Any dimension <5 is an area for improvement.
nodes.practice: Low P: Write 3 grateful things daily; Low E: Use 1 signature strength daily; Low R: Schedule deep conversation with 1 friend weekly; Low M: Do volunteer work; Low A: Set 1 SMART goal.

nodes.label: Broaden-and-Build Theory
nodes.author: Fredrickson
nodes.summary: Good mood does not just feel good — it broadens thinking and builds long-term resources.
nodes.desc: Positive emotions broaden an individual's thought-action repertoire and build lasting personal resources (physical, intellectual, social, psychological). Unlike negative emotions which narrow thinking, positive emotions broaden it: joy makes you want to explore; gratitude makes you want to give back.
examples: Xiao Li receives a birthday gift and feels grateful → proactively helps friends (broadens prosocial behavior) → relationships grow closer (builds social resources)
Fear narrows thinking to escape only; joy broadens thinking to explore and create
nodes.selfTest: Reflect on today: What positive emotion did you experience? What triggered it? What did it make you want to do? Keep a positive emotion diary for 30 days.
nodes.practice: Write a positive emotion diary daily: record emotion type, trigger, and what it made you want to do. Deliberately create more positive moments.

nodes.label: VIA Character Strengths
nodes.author: Peterson & Seligman
nodes.summary: Everyone has 24 character strengths. Find your 'signature strengths' and use them well.
nodes.desc: A classification system of 6 virtues and 24 character strengths that helps individuals identify and develop their signature strengths. The six virtues are: Wisdom & Knowledge, Courage, Humanity, Justice, Temperance, and Transcendence. Working from strengths gives you more energy.
examples: Xiao Zhang's signature strength is creativity → proactively takes on innovative projects, full of passion
Xiao Wang's signature strength is kindness → proactively helps colleagues, becomes the team glue
nodes.selfTest: Visit viacharacter.org to complete the free 15-minute assessment and get your top 5 signature strengths. Or ask yourself: When do you feel 'this is the real me'?
nodes.practice: Choose 1 strength to use deliberately each week. Example: Creativity strength → try a new method for one daily task; Kindness strength → do 1 act of kindness daily.

nodes.label: Growth Mindset
nodes.author: Dweck
nodes.summary: Your abilities are not fixed — they can be improved through effort. This belief changes how you face challenges.
nodes.desc: The belief that abilities can be developed through effort vs. the belief that abilities are fixed. Growth mindset individuals embrace challenges, persist through setbacks, learn from others' success, and view effort as necessary for mastery. Fixed mindset individuals avoid challenges and give up easily when facing obstacles.
examples: Math test failed → Growth: 'Need to change study method'; Fixed: 'I'm too dumb'
Seeing others succeed → Growth: Ask them for advice; Fixed: Feel threatened
nodes.selfTest: Rate statements about fixed mindset (ability cannot be changed / mistakes mean you're unintelligent) and growth mindset (effort improves intelligence / failure is a learning opportunity).
nodes.practice: 1. Notice fixed mindset triggers; 2. Reframe inner dialogue: 'I haven't mastered this yet'; 3. Use 'not yet' language; 4. Praise effort, not ability.

nodes.label: Self-Efficacy Theory
nodes.author: Bandura
nodes.summary: Believing you can do something — this belief itself helps you actually do it.
nodes.desc: An individual's belief in their ability to successfully complete tasks in specific domains. Influenced by four factors: mastery experiences (past successes), vicarious experiences (observing role models), social persuasion (encouragement from others), and physiological/emotional states (interpreting nervousness as readiness).
examples: Two people with same English level give a speech → high self-efficacy performs better
Xiao Zhang: 'I definitely can't do it' → poor performance; Xiao Wang: 'I'm well prepared' → good performance
nodes.selfTest: List 3 life domains (work/study/relationships/health), rate confidence in: completing difficult tasks / coping with setbacks / learning new skills (1-10).
nodes.practice: 1. Create mastery experiences: break big tasks into small steps; 2. Find similar role models; 3. Change self-talk; 4. Reframe nervousness as 'I'm ready.'

nodes.label: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
nodes.author: Beck
nodes.summary: Thoughts, feelings, and behaviors influence each other. Change distorted thinking, and you improve emotions and behaviors.
nodes.desc: CBT holds that psychological problems stem from erroneous cognition (cognitive deficits and cognitive distortions). The core tool is the cognitive triangle: thoughts, feelings, and behaviors mutually influence each other. Common cognitive distortions include all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophizing, mind reading, emotional reasoning, and 11 others.
examples: Friend doesn't reply to WeChat → catastrophizing: 'They don't care about me' → sad and anxious → rational thought: 'They might be busy' → calm
nodes.selfTest: Next time you have a negative emotion, use a thought record: record Situation / Automatic Thought / Emotion Intensity / Cognitive Distortion / More Rational Thought / New Emotion. Persist for 2 weeks.
nodes.practice: Use a thought record to challenge cognitive distortions. Core questions: 'Is there evidence supporting my thought?' 'Is there a more rational way to view this?'

nodes.label: Flow Theory
nodes.author: Csikszentmihalyi
nodes.summary: When you are completely absorbed in something, you experience a 'selfless' optimal state where time flies by.
nodes.desc: Flow is an optimal experience state where an individual is completely absorbed in an activity, containing 8 core components: complete concentration, clear goals, loss of self-consciousness, time distortion, intrinsic reward, challenge-skill balance, sense of control, and action-awareness merging. Flow ≠ relaxation — it is focused challenge.
examples: Playing games / drawing / coding and forgetting to eat, losing track of time, not feeling tired, not worrying about others' opinions — this is flow
nodes.selfTest: Recall the past 3 months: When did you lose track of time? What activity made you feel 'the challenge is just right, not too hard, not too easy'?
nodes.practice: 1. Find flow activities; 2. Create optimal environment: fixed time, phone off, clear goals, immediate feedback; 3. Adjust challenge level; 4. Schedule 30-60 minutes of flow time daily.

nodes.label: Fast and Slow Thinking
nodes.author: Kahneman
nodes.summary: The brain has two systems: fast, intuitive System 1, and slow, rational System 2. Good decisions require both systems working together.
nodes.desc: System 1 (fast, automatic, intuitive) handles pattern recognition and heuristics; System 2 (slow, analytical, deliberate) handles logical reasoning and calculation. System 1 often lazily causes biases such as anchoring effect, availability heuristic, representativeness heuristic, loss aversion, and others.
examples: 2+2=4 → System 1 immediate response; 17×24=? → System 2 needs calculation
Seeing a red light and immediately hitting the brake → System 1; Deciding which computer to buy → System 2
nodes.selfTest: Review recent important decisions: Was it made on intuition? Was it anchored by first impressions? Did you only look at information supporting your view?
nodes.practice: 1. Recognize System 1 moments; 2. Use a decision checklist before important decisions; 3. Seek counter-evidence: actively ask 'What are the reasons it might fail?'

nodes.label: Grit: Passion and Perseverance
nodes.author: Duckworth
nodes.summary: Sustained passion and perseverance toward long-term goals predicts long-term success better than talent.
nodes.desc: Grit consists of two core components: passion (sustained passion and directional consistency toward long-term goals) and perseverance (continuing to work hard even when it's difficult or boring). Research shows Grit predicts academic performance, graduation rates, West Point performance, etc., better than talent.
examples: High talent but inconsistent effort → hard to succeed; Average talent but daily persistence → solo recital after 5 years
nodes.selfTest: Rate 8 statements (1-5): Have clear long-term goals / Passionate about goals for many years / Persist even when bored / Don't give up when facing setbacks, etc.
nodes.practice: 1. Find your 'top-level goal'; 2. Break big goals into small goals; 3. Establish a 'don't give up' ritual: fixed practice time, 5-minute rule; 4. Build a support system.

nodes.label: Self-Determination Theory
nodes.author: Ryan & Deci
nodes.summary: True motivation comes from within, not external rewards. Satisfy the three needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness, and you'll have sustained motivation.
nodes.desc: Human motivation exists on a continuum from controlled motivation to autonomous motivation. Satisfying three basic psychological needs promotes intrinsic motivation: Autonomy (behavior is one's own choice), Competence (ability to cope with challenges), and Relatedness (connection with others). External rewards only provide short-term motivation.
examples: Wife urges quitting smoking → external pressure → easy to relapse; Want to be healthy for the child → internal drive → more likely to persist
nodes.selfTest: Assess your type of motivation for doing something: External regulation (for money / avoid punishment) / Introjected regulation (guilt if not doing) / Identified regulation (aligns with values) / Intrinsic motivation (inherently interesting).
nodes.practice: 1. Recognize controlled motivation; 2. Internalize external motivation: 'I choose to do this because I want to be healthy'; 3. Satisfy three needs: Autonomy (give choice), Competence (reachable goals), Relatedness (do it with friends).

nodes.label: Post-Traumatic Growth
nodes.author: Tedeschi & Calhoun
nodes.summary: After experiencing difficulty and trauma, you may grow in 5 domains and become stronger than before.
nodes.desc: Traumatic events challenge an individual's worldview. Through repeated rumination and coping processes, individuals may experience growth in 5 domains: personal strength, new possibilities, deeper relationships, appreciation of life, and spiritual development. Note: PTG is not 'gratitude for trauma' but 'finding growth after trauma.'
examples: Growth after job loss: discovering you're stronger than you thought / discovering entrepreneurial opportunities / cherishing family more / enjoying small blessings more
nodes.selfTest: Recall a difficult experience and rate positive changes in 5 domains (1-5): personal strength / new possibilities / deeper relationships / appreciation of life / spiritual development.
nodes.practice: 1. Expressive writing: 15-20 minutes daily for 4 consecutive days; 2. Reframe the narrative: from victim to survivor; 3. Find meaning: 'How did this experience make me a better person?'

nodes.label: Prospect Theory
nodes.author: Kahneman & Tversky
nodes.summary: When we make decisions, we don't 'calculate rationally' but are influenced by psychological biases like loss aversion.
nodes.desc: Decision-making under risk and uncertainty follows principles of reference point dependence, loss aversion, and probability weighting. The pain of losing 100 yuan > the pleasure of gaining 100 yuan. Framing effect: the same event described differently leads to different decisions.
examples: Certain gain of 1000 yuan vs 50% chance of gaining 2000 yuan → most choose certain gain
90% survival rate vs 10% mortality rate → same event, different decisions
nodes.selfTest: Review recent important decisions: Did you make conservative choices because of fear of loss? Were you influenced by how information was framed?
nodes.practice: 1. Recognize the frame: describe the choice in another way; 2. Use external perspective: 'If a friend faced this choice, what would I advise?' 3. Consider opportunity cost.

nodes.label: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy
nodes.author: Segal et al.
nodes.summary: Integrates mindfulness training with the cognitive-behavioral framework to prevent depressive relapse and cultivate present-moment awareness and acceptance.
nodes.desc: MBCT consists of an 8-week program: body scan, mindful yoga, breathing awareness, mindful walking, expanding awareness, defusion from thoughts, and self-compassion. The core is to observe ruminative thoughts without getting caught up in them, and integrate mindfulness into daily activities. Especially effective for patients with 3 or more depressive relapses.
examples: When negative thoughts arise, neither fight them nor follow them — just observe them like clouds drifting by — this is cognitive defusion
nodes.selfTest: How much of your day is spent in 'automatic pilot' mode? Eating while thinking about work, walking while thinking about the past? Try mindful awareness of the present moment.
nodes.practice: 1. Daily body scan or breathing awareness; 2. Integrate mindfulness into daily life: mindful eating, mindful walking; 3. Identify early warning signs of depressive relapse.

nodes.label: Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy
nodes.author: Ellis
nodes.summary: It's not the event itself that upsets you, but your thoughts about the event. The ABC model helps you change beliefs.
nodes.desc: ABC Model: A (Activating event) → B (Belief) → C (Consequence). Ellis proposed 11 irrational beliefs, such as 'I must excel in all domains' and 'Others should always treat me fairly.' Through D (Disputation) a new E (Effect) is formed, replacing irrational beliefs with rational ones.
examples: Friend doesn't reply to WeChat → Irrational: 'She doesn't care about me' → sad and anxious → Rational: 'She might be busy' → calm
nodes.selfTest: Next time you feel down, write down A (what happened) / B (what did you tell yourself) / C (emotion and behavior). Identify if there are any irrational beliefs.
nodes.practice: Use the ABCDE model: Identify ABC → D (Disputation: Is there evidence? Is there a more rational way?) → E (New Effect: form a new rational belief).

nodes.label: Stress and Coping Theory
nodes.author: Lazarus & Folkman
nodes.summary: Stress is not a 'bad thing' — it's an event you appraise as a 'threat.' Change the appraisal, and you change the stress response.
nodes.desc: Cognitive appraisal determines stress perception: primary appraisal (Is this a threat or a challenge?) and secondary appraisal (Can I cope?). Coping styles are divided into problem-focused coping (changing the situation) and emotion-focused coping (regulating emotions). Smart people choose both depending on the situation.
examples: Public speaking → appraised as threat: high anxiety, insomnia; appraised as challenge: moderate tension, excitement
nodes.selfTest: Next time you feel stressed, ask yourself: Do I appraise this as a threat or a challenge? Do I believe I can cope? What coping style do I usually use?
nodes.practice: 1. Reframe primary appraisal: 'This is a challenge, I can grow'; 2. Problem-focused: list controllable parts, make an action plan; 3. Emotion-focused: mindfulness, social support, exercise.

nodes.label: Stress Inoculation Training
nodes.author: Meichenbaum
nodes.summary: Like a vaccine, 'inoculate' yourself against stress in advance, so you can cope better when real stress arrives.
nodes.desc: Three-phase training: Conceptualization phase (understand stress response patterns), Skills Acquisition and Rehearsal phase (learn relaxation, cognitive restructuring, problem solving), and Application and Maintenance phase (simulation practice, gradual exposure, self-monitoring). Helps you avoid going blank during real interviews/speeches.
examples: Before an interview: 1. Understand interview stress patterns; 2. Learn deep breathing and positive self-talk; 3. Simulate interview practice → handle the real interview calmly
nodes.selfTest: Choose an upcoming stressful situation. Record: When imagining this situation, what are the physical reactions? What are the thoughts?
nodes.practice: 1. Conceptualization (1 week): record stress triggers and reactions; 2. Skills acquisition (2-3 weeks): practice relaxation, positive self-talk, visualize success; 3. Application (1-2 weeks): simulation practice, gradual exposure.

nodes.label: Transtheoretical Model
nodes.author: Prochaska & DiClemente
nodes.summary: Behavior change doesn't happen overnight — it has 6 stages. At different stages, you need different strategies.
nodes.desc: Six stages of behavior change: Precontemplation (not considering change), Contemplation (considering but not ready), Preparation (intending to change soon), Action (have started changing), Maintenance (sustaining the change), and Termination (no longer tempted to relapse). Don't force action in the 'precontemplation' stage.
examples: Quitting smoking: Precontemplation 'never thought about it' → Contemplation 'considering it' → Preparation 'will quit next month' → Action 'quit for 3 weeks' → Maintenance 'quit for 6 months' → Termination 'don't want to smoke'
nodes.selfTest: Choose a behavior you want to change. Ask yourself: Have I thought about changing? Am I considering but uncertain? Have I started changing? Identify your current stage.
nodes.practice: Precontemplation: understand pros and cons; Contemplation: make a decision balance sheet; Preparation: set a specific date; Action: use specific techniques; Maintenance: identify high-risk situations.

nodes.label: Self-Expansion Model
nodes.author: Aron & Aron
nodes.summary: When you fall in love with someone, your self-concept 'expands' to include the other's resources, perspectives, and identity.
nodes.desc: Self-expansion in close relationships: by building intimate relationships with others, an individual's self-concept expands to gain new perspectives, identities, and resources. Good relationships make you 'bigger'; bad relationships make you 'smaller.' You start thinking about the future using 'we' instead of 'I.'
examples: After falling in love: didn't like hiking but partner likes it → you also fall in love with it; partner is an architect → you start paying attention to architecture; think about the future using 'we'
nodes.selfTest: Rate important relationship (1-5): Makes me try new activities / Gives me new perspectives / Gains new resources / Self feels bigger / Becoming a better version of myself. Average ≥3.5 indicates a healthy relationship.
nodes.practice: 1. Try new things together; 2. Share each other's passions; 3. Build a 'we' narrative: support each other to become better versions of yourselves.
